newsitem.title: USA: Treasuries end 1996 on down note, home sales up.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries end 1996 on down note, home sales up.

text.p: Government bond prices tumbled in the last session of the year Tuesday as investors sold after signs of quickening economic growth fuelled worries about a pickup in inflation.

The bellwether 30-year Treasury fell 1-9/32 to 99-4/32, a drop of $12.8125 on a $1,000 bond, pushing its yield up to 6.64 percent from 6.54 percent on Monday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Kevin Flanagan, first vice president at Dean Witter, said investors reacted to a Commerce Department report that sales of new homes jumped a stronger-than-expected 14.2 percent in November, the steepest rise in more than 3-1/2 years.

In addition, consumer confidence soared in December, jumping to 113.8 from 109.5 in November, the Conference Board said. The business research group said a sharp rise in confidence this year suggests demand will help pave the way for a healthy economy in early 1997.
The drop in prices was exaggerated by holiday-thinned volume, market participants said.

"As we close out the year, investors are growing concerned that we could be gearing up for a better fourth quarter (of 1996) and a better first quarter of 1997 than people were originally thinking," Flanagan said.

While investors clearly grew worried that might mean a pickup in inflation and higher interest rates, analysts said few forecasters were expecting a jump in gross domestic product that would reignite inflation.
Flanagan estimated fourth-quarter GDP grew at a 3.0 percent to 3.5 percent annual rate, compared to a 2.1 percent rate in the third quarter.
The government's initial report on fourth quarter GDP, the broadest measure of the nation's economy, is due in late January.
"Two of the three pieces of data we got today were fundamentally negative for the market," said W. Michael McClure, trading manager at Zions First National Bank Capital Markets in Salt Lake City.
Separately, Chicago-area purchasing managers said their index of regional manufacturing activity was virtually unchanged in December at 57.4 compared with 57.6 in November.
Investors also sold 5- and 10-year bonds, McClure said.
GovPX, a provider of Treasury prices and volume from five of six major broker-dealers, said volume was significantly below that of a typical Tuesday.
Overall, volume stood at $35.9 billion across the board late on Tuesday compared to $27 billion last New Year's Eve.
Trading closed at 2 p.m., about three hours earlier than usual, for the New Year's Eve holiday. Financial markets will be closed on Wednesday for New Year's Day.

In shorter maturities, the three-month bill rate was unchanged at 5.05 percent. Six-month bill rates rose four hundredths of a point to 5.13 percent and one-year bill rates rose five basis points to 5.22 percent.
Two-year notes fell 5/32 to 99-24/32, yielding 5.88 percent compared with 5.80 percent on Monday. The 10-year note fell 29/32 to 100-16/32 to yield 6.43 percent, up from 6.30 percent on Monday.
In the corporate market, prices were quoted down in line with Treasuries, keeping spreads steady, but few trades were reported. Corporate dealers said desks were very thinly staffed.
Analysts said the National Association of Purchasing Management report on December manufacturing activity, due on Thursday morning, would set the tone for the market at the start of 1997.
